title: HOT-tier cluster optimization under production load
summary: Reducing shard pressure and heap contention on a 16-node production cluster without downtime — moving cold data out of the HOT tier and putting durable guardrails on index growth.

sections.challenge: The HOT tier of a 16-node production cluster was carrying far more shards than its heap could comfortably serve. Shard count had grown to 10,150, with a heap density of 78 shards per GB of heap — well past healthy thresholds — driving GC pressure and unstable query latency. Index growth was unbounded: 2,351 indices had no lifecycle guardrails, and roughly 1.2 TB of data that no longer needed HOT-tier performance was still pinned there.
sections.architecture: The plan separated two concerns: relieve the HOT tier now and stop it refilling. Eligible indices were rolled over and migrated toward warm storage via ILM, while a guardrail policy template was applied across the index space so new indices inherit rollover and retention by default. Compression was switched to best_compression (ZSTD) on warm data to recover storage without sacrificing HOT query speed. All changes were staged to keep the cluster green with zero ingest errors throughout.
sections.implementation: An ILM rollover policy template (illustrative of the applied pattern), staged across the index space and paired with a warm-tier codec change to recover storage without touching HOT latency.
sections.results: Cluster remained green with zero ingest errors throughout the migration. 2,351 indices were brought under lifecycle guardrails to prevent regrowth.
lessons: Heap density (shards per GB heap) is a better early-warning signal than raw shard count — it surfaces pressure before latency degrades.
Relief without guardrails regresses: applying ILM templates across the index space mattered more than the one-time migration.
best_compression on warm tiers reclaimed storage with no measurable HOT-tier query cost.
Staging every change to hold the cluster green made the optimization a non-event for ingest — the right outcome for a production system.
